topics.title: Work, energy and power
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to calculate work done in different situations
The students should be able to list different forms of energy
The students should be able to explain the concept of power

Introduction:
We have learned about force and motion in previous lessons. Today we will see how force applied over distance creates work and how this relates to energy and power in our daily lives.

Content:
Work is done when a force moves an object. Work = Force × Distance. Energy is the ability to do work. Forms include kinetic, potential, heat, light and sound. Power is the rate of doing work or using energy, measured in watts. For example, when you carry a bucket of water from the well, you are doing work. The generator that provides light to your home uses electrical energy to do work.

Class activity:
Students will measure the work done when lifting different objects to different heights and calculate the power required.

Evaluation questions:
1. What is the SI unit of work?
2. List three forms of energy.
3. How is power different from work?
4. Calculate the work done when a force of 10N moves an object 5m.

Summary:
Work, energy and power are related concepts that help us understand how things move and change in our world.

topics.title: Electric charges and current
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to identify conductors and insulators
The students should be able to construct simple circuits
The students should be able to measure current in a circuit

Introduction:
Last term we learned about static electricity. Today we will build on that knowledge to understand electric current and how to measure it in simple circuits.

Content:
Electric charges are positive or negative. Like charges repel while opposite charges attract. Current is the flow of electric charges through a conductor. Conductors allow current to flow easily like copper wire, while insulators like plastic prevent current flow. A simple circuit needs a power source, wires, and a component like a bulb. Current is measured in amperes using an ammeter connected in series.

Class activity:
Students will build simple circuits using batteries, wires, bulbs and switches, and measure current at different points.

Evaluation questions:
1. What is the difference between conductors and insulators?
2. Draw a symbol for an ammeter.
3. How should an ammeter be connected in a circuit?
4. Name two materials that are good conductors.

Summary:
Electric current flows through conductors and can be measured to understand how electricity works in our homes and schools.

topics.title: Magnetism review
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to describe magnetic fields
The students should be able to identify uses of magnets
The students should be able to make an electromagnet

Introduction:
We have learned about natural magnets before. Today we will review magnetic fields and learn how to create electromagnets which are very important in many devices we use daily.

Content:
Magnetic fields are areas around a magnet where magnetic forces can be detected. They flow from north to south pole. Magnets have many uses like in door catches, electric motors, and generators. An electromagnet is made by wrapping wire around an iron core and passing electric current through it. The stronger the current, the stronger the magnet. This is how doorbells and some cranes work.

Class activity:
Students will make simple electromagnets using batteries, wire, and iron nails, then test their strength by picking up paper clips.

Evaluation questions:
1. What is the direction of magnetic field lines?
2. Name three devices that use magnets.
3. What do you need to make an electromagnet?
4. How can you make an electromagnet stronger?

Summary:
Magnets create fields and can be natural or artificial, with electromagnets being very useful in many modern technologies.

topics.title: Radioactivity basics
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to identify sources of radiation
The students should be able to list uses of radioactivity
The students should be able to explain safety rules

Introduction:
We have learned about atoms and elements in chemistry. Some elements have unstable atoms that give off radiation, which we will learn about today and how it affects our lives.

Content:
Radioactivity is when unstable atoms release energy to become stable. Sources include uranium, radium, and cobalt. Uses include medical treatment like X-rays, food preservation, and generating electricity in power plants. Dangers include causing cancer and damaging cells. Safety rules include avoiding exposure, using shields like lead or concrete, and proper disposal of radioactive materials. In Nigeria, we follow strict safety guidelines in hospitals and research centers.

Class activity:
Students will create posters showing different uses and safety precautions for radioactive materials.

Evaluation questions:
1. What is radioactivity?
2. Name two uses of radioactivity.
3. How can we protect ourselves from radiation?
4. What element is commonly used in nuclear power plants?

Summary:
Radioactivity has both helpful and dangerous aspects, so we must understand and follow safety rules when using it.

topics.title: Soap making
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to explain saponification
The students should be able to list materials for soap making
The students should be able to make local soap

Introduction:
We use soap every day to clean ourselves and our clothes. Today we will learn how soap is made through a chemical reaction called saponification, and we will make some ourselves.

Content:
Soap making is called saponification. It happens when fats or oils react with a strong alkali like sodium hydroxide. Materials needed include palm oil, shea butter, sodium hydroxide, water, and essential oils for fragrance. The process involves mixing oil and lye solution, then adding scents before pouring into molds to harden. In Nigeria, we often use local palm oil and traditional methods to make black soap and other soaps.

Class activity:
Students will make small batches of local soap using palm oil and sodium hydroxide with teacher supervision.

Evaluation questions:
1. What is saponification?
2. Name two materials needed for soap making.
3. Why do we add essential oils to soap?
4. What safety precautions should we take when making soap?

Summary:
Soap is made through saponification, a chemical reaction between fats and alkalis, and is an important part of our daily hygiene.

topics.title: Metals and alloys
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to list properties of metals
The students should be able to identify common alloys
The students should be able to sort metals based on properties

Introduction:
We see metals everywhere in our lives, from pots and pans to bridges and coins. Today we will learn about the properties of metals and how they can be combined to make alloys with special characteristics.

Content:
Metals are shiny, good conductors of heat and electricity, and can be hammered into shapes without breaking. Common metals include iron, copper, aluminum, and zinc. Alloys are mixtures of metals, like bronze (copper and tin), brass (copper and zinc), and steel (iron with carbon). Alloys are often stronger and more useful than pure metals. In Nigeria, we use aluminum for roofing, iron for construction, and copper for electrical wiring.

Class activity:
Students will be given samples of different metals and alloys to test properties like conductivity and magnetism, then sort them into categories.

Evaluation questions:
1. Name three properties of metals.
2. What is an alloy?
3. Name one alloy and its components.
4. Why are alloys often better than pure metals?

Summary:
Metals have useful properties that can be improved by making alloys, which are essential in our technology and construction.

topics.title: Ceramics and glass
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to explain how ceramics are made
The students should be able to list uses of ceramics and glass
The students should be able to perform a clay experiment

Introduction:
From the pots our grandparents used to cook with to the windows in our classrooms, ceramics and glass play important roles in our daily lives. Today we will learn how these materials are made and used.

Content:
Ceramics are made from clay shaped and then fired in a kiln at high temperatures. This makes them hard and durable. Examples include pots, tiles, and bricks. Glass is made from sand, soda ash, and limestone melted at very high temperatures. It can be molded into different shapes. Uses include windows, bottles, and mirrors. In Nigeria, traditional pottery is an important art form, and we use glass for windows, bottles, and decorative items.

Class activity:
Students will shape clay into simple pots and observe how it changes after drying and firing (using a school kiln).

Evaluation questions:
1. What is ceramics made from?
2. How is glass made?
3. Name two uses of ceramics.
4. What happens to clay when it is fired?

Summary:
Ceramics and glass are important materials made from natural substances that become useful through heating and shaping processes.

topics.title: Plastics and rubber
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to differentiate between thermoplastics and thermosets
The students should be able to identify recycling codes
The students should be able to explain the importance of recycling

Introduction:
Plastics and rubber are materials we use every day from our phone cases to the tires on our vehicles. Today we will learn about different types and how we can manage them responsibly.

Content:
Thermoplastics soften when heated and can be reshaped, like polyethylene bags and PVC pipes. Thermosets harden permanently when heated, like bakelite and rubber tires. Plastics have recycling codes from 1-7 inside triangles to help identify their type. Recycling plastics reduces waste and pollution. In Nigeria, we see plastic bottles everywhere, and learning to recycle them helps our environment and can create economic opportunities.

Class activity:
Students will collect plastic items, identify their recycling codes, and sort them into appropriate recycling categories.

Evaluation questions:
1. What is the difference between thermoplastics and thermosets?
2. What do the numbers 1-7 on plastics mean?
3. Name two thermoplastics.
4. Why is recycling plastics important?

Summary:
Understanding different types of plastics and rubber helps us use them wisely and recycle to protect our environment.

topics.title: Nano and space technology
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to explain nanotechnology
The students should be able to list applications of space technology
The students should be able to discuss benefits of these technologies

Introduction:
The world of technology is always advancing with new frontiers in very small and very large scales. Today we will explore nanotechnology and space technology which represent the cutting edge of science.

Content:
Nanotechnology involves working with materials at the nanometer scale (one billionth of a meter). It has applications in medicine, electronics, and materials science. Space technology includes satellites, rockets, and space stations. It helps with communication, weather forecasting, and GPS navigation. In Nigeria, we benefit from space technology through communication satellites and weather monitoring that help farmers predict rainfall patterns.

Class activity:
Students will research and give short presentations on either nanotechnology applications in medicine or how space technology helps Nigeria.

Evaluation questions:
1. What is nanotechnology?
2. Name two applications of space technology.
3. How does nanotechnology help medicine?
4. How does space technology help Nigerian farmers?

Summary:
Nanotechnology and space technology are advancing fields that bring many benefits to our daily lives and help solve global challenges.

topics.title: Revision and BECE practice
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to answer past BECE questions
The students should be able to identify common mistakes
The students should be able to improve exam techniques

Introduction:
We have covered many topics this term. Today we will practice answering questions similar to what you will see in your BECE examination to help you prepare and improve your performance.

Content:
We will review past BECE questions from topics covered this term including work, energy, electricity, magnetism, radioactivity, soap making, metals, ceramics, glass, plastics, rubber, nanotechnology and space technology. We will discuss common mistakes students make and strategies for answering different types of questions correctly.

Class activity:
Students will work in groups to solve past BECE questions, then present their answers to the class for discussion and correction.

Evaluation questions:
1. Explain how to measure current in a circuit.
2. Describe how to make an electromagnet.
3. What are the safety rules for handling radioactive materials?
4. Explain the difference between thermoplastics and thermosets.

Summary:
Regular practice with past questions helps improve exam performance and identifies areas that need more revision.
